title: Commons Lexicon Term
description: One entry in the Commons Lexicon (RFC 0039): the shared vocabulary of the two MADFAM hyperobject commons. A term is the canonical, quadrilingual definition of a word that both commons — and third-party cartridge authors — use. Terms are born quadrilingual: en/es/fr/pt are ALL required to ship (RFC 0039 §7), because a partial entry is a translation debt that never gets paid. A term is also where a geometry lesson becomes durable: `constraints` carries the clamp rule or degeneracy trap that would otherwise live only in a code comment and be copied, bug and all, into the next cartridge (the case that motivated this schema: fashion-cabinet #113).

spec_version.description: Version of THIS term contract the entry is written against. Absent means 1. Contract 2 (RFC 0039 G2/G3) is ADDITIVE over 1: it adds the optional `review_status` block and the `capability` domain, so every contract-1 entry is still valid and unchanged. An entry declares 2 when it uses either.

id.description: Stable kebab-case id, globally unique across the lexicon. It is what `see_also` points at and what a platform's define(term) tool resolves, so it is a published name: renaming one is a breaking change.

domain.description: Which part of the commons the term belongs to. A controlled list spanning both halves — the solid side (yantra4d), the soft side (fashion-cabinet), and the shared seams between them.

term.description: The word itself in each language. All four are required: this is the dictionary headword, and an entry missing one is not shippable (RFC 0039 §7).

definition.description: What the term means, in each language. Written to be read by a contributor who does not already know — a definition that only makes sense to someone who knows the answer is not a definition.

aliases.description: The SAME concept as it is actually spelled in each repo. This is how the lexicon absorbs a dialect split rather than papering over it: FC's `zipper_tape` and Yantra4D's `tape_edge` are one term with two recorded dialects, and each alias names the repo where that spelling is real, so a reader who arrives holding either word lands on the same entry.

standards.description: Published standards the term is defined against, cited by their identifier (e.g. 'ISO 8559-1'). Optional — most house vocabulary has no standard, and inventing one is worse than having none.

embodied_by.description: Cartridges where the term is real, as '<repo>/<slug>'. The lexicon's claim to be about actual objects rather than about words rests on this field: a term nothing embodies is a term nobody needed.

see_also.description: Other term ids in this lexicon. Validated — a dangling cross-reference is a broken dictionary, so the lane refuses it.

constraints.description: The rule that comes with the term: a clamp, a degeneracy trap, a bound that must hold. Free text, in English, and deliberately singular — if a term needs three, it is probably three terms. This is the field that pays for the lexicon.

heritage.description: True when the entry makes a cultural or historical claim. Setting it engages RFC 0039 §7's citation bar: a heritage term MUST carry at least one source, and the lane fails the entry otherwise. It is a self-declared flag on purpose — the author knows they are making the claim.

sources.description: Citations backing the entry's claims. REQUIRED when `heritage` is true (RFC 0039 §7: no uncited cultural or historical claim). A citation is a string a reader can follow: a publication, a standard, a repo path, or an issue reference.

review_status.description: Whether the four language facets have had a native review pass, or are still the drafting pass that wrote them. RFC 0039 §5 allows machine or agent drafting as a DRAFT and never as shipped copy without a review; §7 asks that fr/pt be reviewed rather than merely generated. A generated entry is still shippable — quadrilingual completeness is the ship gate, not review — but it must never read as reviewed, so an entry drafted in one pass says so here and the status line counts it separately. Absent means unmarked: the G1 corpus predates this block and does not claim either way.

notes.description: Anything true and worth saying that is not the definition — where the equivalence stops, what the term is often confused with.

reviewState.description: `generated` — written in a drafting pass (by a contributor or an agent) and not yet checked by a speaker of the language. `reviewed` — a named reviewer has read it in that language and let it stand.

state.description: The entry's overall state — the WORST of its language facets, never the best. Claiming `reviewed` also requires at least one named reviewer: a review nobody signed is the failure mode this field exists to prevent.

languages.description: Per-language state, for the ordinary case where the review pass lands one language at a time. Optional; absent means `state` speaks for all four.

reviewers.description: Who reviewed, as a name or handle a reader can ask. Required for `state: reviewed`.

note.description: What the drafting pass was unsure of — the sentence a reviewer should look at first.

cartridgeSlug.description: '<repo>/<slug>', where repo is one of the two commons.

quadrilingualString.description: A string in all four languages of the commons (RFC 0039, ruled 2026-08-25). Spanish is the house register and the quality bar; French and Portuguese are reviewed, not merely generated.

name.description: The identifier as it literally appears in that repo's data (e.g. 'zipper_tape').

note.description: What the spelling is (a manifest enum value, a parameter id, drafting idiom) and why it differs.
